cards.back: DTIME$(t(n))$ is the class of all languages that can be decided by a deterministic single-tape Turing Machine in $O(t(n))$ time, where $n$ is the length of the input. Time refers to the total number of steps the TM takes.

DSPACE$(s(n))$ is the class of all languages that can be decided by a deterministic single-tape Turing Machine using $O(s(n))$ space, where $n$ is the length of the input. Space refers to the number of distinct tape cells accessed by the TM.

cards.front: What is the complexity class P, and what kind of problems does it contain?
cards.back: P (Polynomial Time) is the class of languages decidable by a deterministic Turing Machine in polynomial time. Formally, $P = \bigcup_{k \ge 1} \text{DTIME}(n^k)$. It contains problems considered "efficiently solvable" or "tractable," such as sorting, searching, and reachability in graphs.

cards.front: What is the complexity class PSPACE, and how does it relate to P?
cards.back: PSPACE (Polynomial Space) is the class of languages decidable by a deterministic Turing Machine using polynomial space. Formally, $PSPACE = \bigcup_{k \ge 1} \text{DSPACE}(n^k)$. All problems in P are also in PSPACE, meaning $P \subseteq PSPACE$. This is because a TM running in polynomial time can only visit a polynomial number of tape cells.

cards.front: State Savitch's Theorem and its implications for space complexity.
cards.back: Savitch's Theorem states that for any function $s(n) \ge \log n$, $\text{NSPACE}(s(n)) \subseteq \text{DSPACE}(s(n)^2)$. This implies that deterministic Turing Machines can simulate nondeterministic ones with only a polynomial increase in space. For example, $NPSPACE = PSPACE$.

cards.front: Explain why $DTIME(t(n)) \subseteq DSPACE(t(n))$ for any time-constructible function $t(n)$.
cards.back: A deterministic Turing Machine operating for $t(n)$ steps can write on at most $t(n)$ distinct tape cells. Each step involves reading/writing one cell and potentially moving. Thus, the total space used cannot exceed the total time taken. Therefore, any language decidable in $O(t(n))$ time is also decidable in $O(t(n))$ space.

cards.front: What does the Space Hierarchy Theorem state, and what is its significance?
cards.back: For any space-constructible function $s(n)$, there exists a language $L$ that is decidable in $O(s(n))$ space but not in $o(s(n))$ space. More precisely, if $s_1(n)$ and $s_2(n)$ are space-constructible functions such that $s_1(n) = o(s_2(n))$, then $\text{DSPACE}(s_1(n)) \subsetneq \text{DSPACE}(s_2(n))$. It signifies that giving a TM asymptotically more space allows it to solve strictly more problems.

cards.front: Define the complexity classes L and EXP.
cards.back:
L (Logarithmic Space): $L = \text{DSPACE}(\log n)$. This class contains problems solvable by a deterministic TM using only logarithmic space.
EXP (Exponential Time): $EXP = \bigcup_{k \ge 1} \text{DTIME}(2^{n^k})$. This class contains problems solvable by a deterministic TM in exponential time.

cards.front: Order the following complexity classes from smallest to largest, indicating known strict inclusions: L, P, PSPACE, EXP, EXPSPACE.
cards.back:
The known hierarchy is: $L \subseteq P \subseteq PSPACE \subseteq EXP \subseteq EXPSPACE$.
Known strict inclusions:
- $L \subsetneq PSPACE$
- $P \subsetneq EXP$
- $PSPACE \subsetneq EXPSPACE$
It is an open problem whether $L \subsetneq P$ or $P \subsetneq PSPACE$ (at least one must be strict).
